\label{def:treept}
	Given a digraph $D$, a triple $(T,\beta,\gamma)$ is a {\em{tree-partition}} of $D$ if $T$ is a tree and we have the following:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(P\arabic*)},leftmargin=1.2cm]
		\item \(\beta \colon 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi \to 2^{
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi}\) maps every node $x$ of \(T\) to a subset of vertices \(\beta(x)\subseteq 
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi\), called the \emph{bag} of $x$, so that $\{\beta(x)\colon x\in 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi\}$ is a near-partition of \(
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi\).\label{item:tp:bags}
		\item \(\gamma \colon 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi \to 2^{A(D)}\) maps every edge~$e=xy$ of \(T\) to a set of edges \(\gamma(e)\subseteq A(D)\), called the \emph{edge-guard} of~$e$, so that \(\gamma(e)\) hits all the cycles in $D$ that cross the cut induced by $e$; i.e.,  $(\beta({T}^{x}_{e}),\beta({T}^{y}_{e}))$.\label{item:tp:edgeguards}
	\end{enumerate}
	The \emph{porosity} of $(T,\beta,\gamma)$ is the maximum size of an edge-guard, that is, $\max_{e\in E(T)} |\gamma(e)|$.

body_md:
\label{def:dtw}
	A \emph{directed tree-decomposition} of a digraph \(D\) is a triple \(\mathchoice{\left( T, \beta, \gamma \right)}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}\), where \(T\) is a rooted tree, and \(\beta\colon V(T) \to 2^{V(D)}\) and \(\gamma\colon E(T) \to 2^{V(D)}\) are functions mapping every node $x$ of \(T\) to its \emph{bag} $\beta(x)\subseteq 
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi$, and every edge $e$ of \(T\) to its \emph{guard} \(\gamma(e)\subseteq D\), so that the following conditions are satisfied.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(T\arabic*)},leftmargin=1.2cm]
		\item \label{item:directed-tree-width:beta}
		\(\Set{\beta(x) \colon x \in V(T)}\) is a near-partition of \(V(D)\); and
		\item \label{item:directed-tree-width:guard}
		for every \(e \in 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi\), there is no cycle in \(D - \gamma(e)\) visiting both \(\beta({T}^{\downarrow}_{e})\) and~\(\beta({T}^{\uparrow}_{e})\).
	\end{enumerate}
	For \(x \in V(T)\) we define \(\Gamma(x) \coloneqq \beta(x) \cup \bigcup \set{\gamma(e) : e \sim x}\).
	The \emph{width} of \(\mathchoice{\left( T, \beta, \gamma \right)}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}{( T, \beta, \gamma )}\) is the least integer \(w\) such that \(\Abs{\Gamma(t)} \leqslant w + 1\) for all \(t \in V(T)\).
	The \emph{directed treewidth\xspace} of \(D\) is the smallest width of any directed tree-decomposition of \(D\).

	Now define \(\gamma\colon E(T)\to 2^{V(D)}\) mapping every edge \(e=xy\) of \(T\) to a minimum vertex set \(\gamma(e) \subseteq

	\operatorname{dbw}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \((T, \beta, \gamma, \theta)\) be a directed tree-cut-decomposition\xspace of \(D\) of optimum width, and
	let \(\mu\) be an immersion model of \(D'\) in \(D\).
	Let us define a new bag function \(\beta' \colon V(T) \rightarrow 2^{V(D')}\) by setting \[\beta'(x) \coloneqq \mu^{-1}(\beta(x)),\qquad\text{for every node }x\text{ of }T.\]
	                                                    
	Further, for a set of edges \(F \subseteq E(D)\) we define
	\[\zeta(F) \coloneqq \set{e \in E(D') \mid \mu(e) \cap F \neq \emptyset}.\]
	Observe that for any \(F \subseteq E(D)\) we have \(\Abs{\zeta(F)} \leqslant \Abs{F}\), as the trails used by \(\mu\) are
	pairwise edge-disjoint by definition.
	So, we finally define \(\gamma' \colon E(T) \rightarrow 2^{E(D')}\),
	and \(\theta' \colon V(T) \rightarrow 2^{E(D')}\) by setting, for each $e\in E(T)$ and $x\in V(T)$
	\begin{equation*}
		\gamma'(e) \coloneqq \zeta(\gamma(e))\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\theta'(x) \coloneqq \zeta(\theta(x))\text{.}
	\end{equation*}
	We now argue that \((T, \beta', \gamma', \theta')\) is a directed tree-cut-decomposition\xspace of \(D'\). First, to argue \cref{item:dtcw:tp} we have to check that $(T, \beta', \gamma')$ is a tree-partition of $D'$.
	Clearly, \(\beta'\) is a near-partition of \(V(D')\), so \cref{item:tp:bags} holds.
	To argue \cref{item:tp:edgeguards}, consider any edge \(e = xy\) of \(T\).
	Let \(A \coloneqq \beta({T}^{x}_{e})\), \(B \coloneqq \beta({T}^{y}_{e})\),
	\(A' \coloneqq \beta'({T}^{x}_{e})\), and \(B' \coloneqq \beta'({T}^{y}_{e})\). Further,
	let \(C\) be a cycle in \(D'\) crossing the cut \((A',B')\),
	and let \(F \coloneqq \gamma(e)\) and \(F' \coloneqq \gamma'(e)\).
	Observe that \(\mu(E(C))\) is the edge set of a cycle (not necessarily simple) in \(D\)
	that crosses the cut $(A,B)$.
	Therefore, $C$ must contain an edge \(f \in F\).
	This edge must be contained in some \(\mu(f')\) where \(f' \in E(C)\),
	and therefore we have $f'\in F'\cap E(C)$; so $C$ is hit by $F'$. This establishes \cref{item:tp:edgeguards} and thereby also \cref{item:dtcw:tp}.
	The proof of \cref{item:dtcw:onionguards} follows similar lines as that of \cref{item:tp:edgeguards}; we leave it to the reader.
	                                                                           
	                                                           
	
	From the construction it follows immediately that the width of \((T, \beta', \gamma', \theta')\)
	is at most that of \((T, \beta, \gamma, \theta)\). As the width of \((T, \beta, \gamma, \theta)\) is equal to the directed tree-cutwidth of $D$, this proves that the directed tree-cutwidth of $D'$ is bounded by the directed tree-cutwidth of $D$.

label: lemma:porosity-boolean
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:porosity-boolean}
  Let \(D\) be a digraph, \((A,B), (A',B')\) be cuts in \(D\), and $p,p'$ be the porosity of \((A,B)\) and \(A',B'\), respectively.
  Then \((A \cup A', B \cap B'), (A \cap A', B \cup B'), (A \cap B', B \cup A'), (A' \cap B, B' \cup A)\)
  are all cuts in \(D\) of porosity at most \(p+p'\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the porosity of \((A,B)\) is the same as that of \((B,A)\),
  and the roles of \((A,B)\) and \((A',B')\) are symmetric,
  it suffices to argue about \((A \cap A', B \cup B')\).

  Let \(F\) be the set of \(p\) edges hitting all cycles visiting  both \(A\) and \(B\), and let \(F'\) be the set of \(p'\) edges hitting all cycles visiting both \(A'\) and \(B'\).
  We argue next that \(F \cup F'\) hits all cycles containing a vertex of both \(A \cap A'\) and \(B \cup B'\).
  Let \(C\) be such a cycle.
  It contains a vertex \(a \in A \cap A'\), and a vertex \(b \in B \cup B'\).
  If \(b \in B\), then the cycle contains a vertex of both \(A\) and \(B\) and thus is hit by \(F\).
  If \(b \in B'\) then \(C\) contains a vertex of \(A'\) and a vertex of \(B'\) and thus is hit by \(F'\).

label: lemma:porosity-onecl
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:porosity-onecl}
  Let \(D\) be a digraph and let \((A,B)\) be a cut in \(D\).
  Let \(X \subseteq A\) and \(A' \coloneqq \ensuremath{\text{closure}_{D[A]}\Paren*{X}}\).
  Then the porosity of the cut \((A', V(D) - A')\)
  is at most the porosity of the cut \((A,B)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(F\) be any set of edges hitting all cycles visiting both \(A\) and \(B\).
  We now argue that \(F\) is also a hitting set for cycles visiting both \(A'\) and \(V(D) - A'\).

  Let \(C\) be a cycle visiting a vertex \(a \in A' \subseteq A\) and \(b \in V(D) - A'\).
  This cycle clearly contains a vertex of \(A\).
  Observe, however, that \(C\) cannot be entirely contained in $D[A]$, since then \(b\) would also be a member of the closure of \(X\) within \(D[A]\), that is, of $A'$.
                                      
                                                
                                         
                                              
                                                   
                                                    
                                                       
                                                      
                                          
                                              
                                               
                                                   
  So \(C\) must visit \(B\), and thus, is a cycle crossing the cut $(A,B)$, that therefore is hit by \(F\).

body_md:
\label{lem:partial_potatoes}
	Let \(D\) be a digraph and \(S \subseteq 
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi\) a \(k\)-flow-connected set.
	Then, there exists a partial tree-partition \((T, \beta, \eta)\) of \(S\) in \(D\),
  where each \(\beta(x)\), for \(x \in V(T)\) is a \((k + 1)\)-flow-connected set.
	Furthermore, all cuts \(\eta(e)\), for \(e \in E(T)\), have order \(k\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(S = \emptyset\), then \(S\) is already \((k + 1)\)-flow-connected,
	and we simply set
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(T\) to be a single-node tree,
		\item \(\beta\) to map the single node to the empty set,
		\item \(\eta\) to be the empty mapping, and
	\end{itemize} 
	Let us assume henceforth that \(S\) is not empty, and fix any \(s \in S\).
	                                                                              
	Note that since \(S\) is $k$-flow-connected, every cut of $D$ that splits $S$ has order at least~$k$.
	
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
	Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be an inclusion-wise maximal family of cuts of $D$ of order \(k\) that is laminar on \(S\).
	By reverting every cut in \(\mathcal{F}\) if necessary we may assume that for each $(A,B)\in \mathcal{F}$, we have $s\notin A$ (and thus $s\in B$).
	Let \(\sim_\mathcal{F}\) be the following equivalence relation on \(S\):
	\(u \sim_\mathcal{F} v\) if and only if no cut in \(\mathcal{F}\) splits \(\Set{u,v}\).
	                                                                                    
	Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the set of equivalence classes under~\(\sim_\mathcal{F}\).
	
	\begin{claim}
		\label{potlemma:claim:connectivity}
		Every element \(X\) of \(\mathcal{X}\) is \((k + 1)\)-flow-connected in $D$.
	\end{claim}
	\begin{claimproof}
		Suppose this not the case and we have \(u,v \in X\) and a cut
		\((A, B)\) of order \(k\) in \(D\) such that \(u \in A\) and  \(v \in B\).
		Without loss of generality, assume that \(\Abs{
	\ifx\relax A\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\!\mathchoice{\left( A \right)}{( A )}{( A )}{( A )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A \right)}{( A )}{( A )}{( A )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A \right)}{( A )}{( A )}{( A )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A \right)}{( A )}{( A )}{( A )}}
                     
	\fi} = k\).
		Since no cut in \(\mathcal{F}\) splits \(\Set{u,v}\) while \((A, B)\) does,
		this in particular means that \((A, B) \not\in \mathcal{F}\) and \((B,A)\notin \mathcal{F}\).
		Let us exploit this
		fact to exhibit a larger family of \(k\)-cuts that is laminar on \(S\).
		
		We construct a sequence of cuts \(F_0, F_1, \dots\).
		Let us start with \(F_0 = (A, B)\).
		We ensure that our sequence maintains the following invariants on each cut \(F_i = (A_i, B_i)\):
		\begin{itemize}
			\item \(\Abs{
	\ifx\relax A_i\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\!\mathchoice{\left( A_i \right)}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A_i \right)}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A_i \right)}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A_i \right)}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}{( A_i )}}
                     
	\fi}= k\);
			\item \(u \in A_i\) and \(v \in B_i\); and
			\item when \(i > 0\), if a cut \((A',B') \in \mathcal{F}\) does not cross
			with \(F_{i - 1}\) on \(S\), then it also does not cross with \(F_i\) on \(S\).
		\end{itemize}
		Suppose we have already defined \(F_i = (A_i, B_i)\).
		If the family \(\mathcal{F} \cup \Set{F_i}\) is laminar on \(S\), then the process terminates and we have arrived at a contradiction with the maximality of $\mathcal{F}$; note here that $F_i$ splits $\{u,v\}$ while no other cut of $\mathcal{F}$ does, so the cuts of $\mathcal{F} \cup \Set{F_i}$ have pairwise different intersections with~$S$.
		So, suppose that \((A_i, B_i)\) crosses some \((A', B') \in \mathcal{F}\) on $S$. Without loss of generality assume that
		\(\Abs{
	\ifx\relax A'\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\!\mathchoice{\left( A' \right)}{( A' )}{( A' )}{( A' )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A' \right)}{( A' )}{( A' )}{( A' )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A' \right)}{( A' )}{( A' )}{( A' )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( A' \right)}{( A' )}{( A' )}{( A' )}}
                     
	\fi} = k\).
		Apply~\cref{lemma:potato_uncrossing} to \((A_i , B_i)\),
		\((A', B')\) and the set \(S\).
		In outcome~\cref{lemma:potato_uncrossing:out_uninteresting} we get either:
		\(A_i \cap S \subseteq B' \cap S\), or \(B' \cap S \subseteq A_i \cap S\).
		Either way, we get a contradiction that the two cuts were crossing on \(S\).
		Thus we must get outcome~\cref{lemma:potato_uncrossing:out_uncrossing}.
		If \(u \in A'\) then let us set \(F_{i + 1} =(A_{i+1,B_{i+1}})\coloneqq (A_i \cap A', B_i \cup B')\),
		and otherwise let us set \(F_{i + 1} =(A_{i+1,B_{i+1}})\coloneqq (A_i \cup A', B_i \cap B')\).
		By~\cref{lemma:potato_uncrossing}, \(F_{i + 1}\) is a cut of order k.
		By construction and by the fact that $(A',B')\in \mathcal{F}$ does not split $\{u,v\}$, we have \(u \in A_{i+1}\) and \(v \in B_{i+1}\). 
		Thus first two invariants hold. We also note that, clearly, \(C_{i + 1}\)
		does not cross \((A', B')\).
		We must argue the third invariant.
		
		Let \((A'', B'')\in \mathcal{F}\) be a cut that does not cross \(F_i\) on \(S\).
		Without loss of generality, let \(A''\) be the side that does not contain \(u\) and \(v\).
		Assume first that \(A'\) is the side of \((A', B')\) not containing \(u\) and \(v\).
		Then, by construction, \(A_{i + 1} = A_{i} \cup A'\).
		If \(A_{i}\cap S\) contains \(A''\cap S \) then so does \(A_{i + 1}\cap S\), and $(A'',B'')$ and $F_{i+1}$ do not cross on $S$.
		So \(A_i\cap S\) and \(A''\cap S\) are disjoint. 
		Now, there are three cases to consider: 
		\begin{itemize}
			\item If \(A'\cap S\) and \(A''\cap S\) are disjoint as well, then so are \(A_{i + 1}\cap S\) and \(A''\cap S\), and again $(A'',B'')$ and $F_{i+1}$ do not cross on $S$.
			\item If \(A'\cap S \subseteq A''\cap S\), then \(A_i\cap S\) and \(A'\cap S\) are disjoint (due to \(A_i\cap S\) and \(A''\cap S\) being disjoint), so $F_i$ and $(A',B')$ were not crossing on $S$ to begin with; a contradiction.
			\item Finally, if \(A''\cap S \subseteq A'\cap S\), then \(A''\cap S \subseteq A_{i + 1}\cap S\) and again, $(A'',B'')$ and $F_{i+1}$ do not cross on~$S$.
		\end{itemize}    
		The case in which \(B'\) is the side of \((A', B')\) not containing \(u\) and \(v\) follows by a symmetric argument.
		
		Since in each step the cut \(F_{i + 1}\) crosses on $S$ with at least one cut less than \(F_{i}\) does, the process must terminate in a finite number of steps giving
		the desired contradiction.
	\end{claimproof}
	
	As $\mathcal{F}$ is laminar on $S$, we have that \(\mathcal{F}|_S\) is laminar, hence we may define
	\begin{equation*}
		(T,\lambda,\eta') \coloneqq \mathsf{LaminarTree}(\mathcal{F}|_S,s).
	\end{equation*}
	Let $r$ be the root of $T$.                                                                                                                                             
	                                             
	                                                   
	We endow $T$ with a bag function \(\beta \colon V(T)\to 2^{S}\) defined as follows:
	\begin{equation*}
		\beta(t) \coloneqq \lambda(t) - \bigcup_{c\colon \text{ child of } t\text{ in }T} \lambda(c),\qquad\text{for every }t\in V(T)\text{.}
	\end{equation*}
	\begin{claim}\label{potlemma:near-partition}
		For every node \(t \in V(T)\), the set \(\beta(t)\) is either empty or satisfies
		\(\beta(t) \in \mathcal{X}\).
		Moreover, for every element \(X \in \mathcal{X}\) there is an unique node
		\(t_X \in V(T)\) such that \(\beta(t_X) = X\).
	\end{claim}
	\begin{claimproof}
		First, we verify that \(\{\beta(t)\colon t\in V(T)\}\) is a near-partition of \(S\).
		Consider any \(u \in S\) and suppose \(u \in \beta(t)\)
		and \(u \in \beta(t')\) for some distinct $t,t'\in V(T)$.
		It follows that \(u \in \lambda(t)\) and \(u \in \lambda(t')\),
		so either \(t\) is a descendant of \(t'\)
		or \(t'\) is a descendant of \(t\).
		Without loss of generality, assume the former.
		Let \(t''\) be the child of \(t'\) that is an ancestor of $t$.
		It follows that \(u \in \lambda(t'')\subseteq \lambda(t')\), and
		thus, by construction, \(u \not \in \beta(t)\); a contradiction.
		So \(\{\beta(t)\colon t\in V(T)\}\)	is a near-partition of \(S\).
		
		Note that for any node \(t \in V(T)\) we have
		\[\bigcup_{t'\colon \text{ a descendant of } t\text{ in }T} \beta(t') = \lambda(t)\text{.}\]
		Hence, if \(e=(t,c) \in E(T)\) (so \(t\) is the parent of \(c\)) and
		\((A,B) = \eta((t,c)) \in \mathcal{F}|_S\) with \(s \not \in A\), then we have
		\(A = \lambda(z)\) and consequently
		\(A = \beta({(T)}^{\downarrow}_{e})\), \(B = \beta({(T)}^{\uparrow}_{e})\).
		
		Observe now, that if $u \sim_\mathcal{F} v$, then there must exist $t\in V(T)$ with $u,v\in \beta(t)$.
		Indeed, otherwise there would be an edge $e\in E(T)$ such that $u$ and $v$ belong to the opposite sides of the cut $(\beta({(T)}^{\downarrow}_{e}),\beta({(T)}^{\uparrow}_{e}))=\eta'(e)$, implying that $\{u,v\}$ would be split by $\eta'(e)\in \mathcal{F}|_S$;
		a contradiction to $u\sim_\mathcal{F} v$.
		Consequently, every element of $\mathcal{X}$ is entirely contained in a single element of the near-partition \(\{\beta(t)\colon t\in V(T)\}\).
		
		It now remains to show that if $u,v\in S$ are such that \(u \nsim_\mathcal{F} v\), then $u,v$ belong to different parts of the near-partition \(\{\beta(t)\colon t\in V(T)\}\).
		Since $u\nsim_\mathcal{F} v$, there is a cut \((A,B) \in \mathcal{F}|_S\) such that $u$ and $v$ belong to the opposite sides of $(A,B)$.
		Since $\eta$ is a bijection, there is an edge \(e \in E(T)\) such that \(\eta'(e) = (A,B)\).
		It follows that the nodes whose bags contain $u$ and $v$ must belong to different components of \(T - e\), so these nodes in particular must be different.
		This ends the proof.
	\end{claimproof}
	
	Choosing \(\eta\) as the unique extension in \(\mathcal{F}\) of the cuts in \(\eta'\) to cuts in \(D\) finishes this proof
  (note that this is possible as \(\Abs*{\mathcal{F}} = \Abs*{\mathcal{F}|_S}\))

body_md:
Let \((\widehat{T},\widehat{\lambda})\) be an directed branch-decomposition of \(D\) of width at most \(w\).
	Thus there exists a vertex-guard \(\widehat{\gamma}(e)\) of size at most \(w\) for every \(e \in 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	For a vertex \(v \in V(D)\), let \(h(v)\) be a set of at most \(d\) edges of \(D\)
	that hits all cycles containing \(v\).
	
	We define a directed tree-cut-decomposition\xspace \(\mathchoice{\left( T,\beta,\gamma,\theta \right)}{( T,\beta,\gamma,\theta )}{( T,\beta,\gamma,\theta )}{( T,\beta,\gamma,\theta )}\) of \(D\) using the following formulas, for all $x\in V(T)$ and $e\in E(T)$:
	\begin{align*}
		T &\coloneqq \widehat{T};\\
		\beta(x) &\coloneqq \begin{cases*}
			\Set{\widehat{\lambda}(x)} & \text{if \(x\) is a leaf,}\\
			\emptyset & \text{otherwise;}
		\end{cases*}\\
		\gamma(e) &\coloneqq \bigcup \set{h(v) \colon v \in \widehat{\gamma}(e)};\\
		\theta(x) &\coloneqq \bigcup_{e \sim x} \gamma(e).
	\end{align*}
	
	We now argue that this yields a valid directed tree-cut-decomposition\xspace.
	\Cref{item:tp:bags} is obvious, as the mapping \(\widehat{\lambda}\) bijectively maps \(V(D)\) to the set of leaves of \(T\).
	To argue \cref{item:tp:edgeguards}, take any edge \(e \in E(T)\). The cuts induced by this edge in \((T,\beta)\)
	and in \((T,\widehat{\lambda})\) are the same. Thus, any cycle \(C\) crossing this cut contains a vertex \(v \in \widehat{\lambda}(e)\) by the definition of directed branchwidth.
	Thus it contains some edge \(f \in h(v)\), and thus also of \(\gamma(e)\); so this establishes \cref{item:tp:edgeguards}, and hence also \cref{item:dtcw:tp}.
	To argue~\cref{item:dtcw:onionguards}, consider any \(x \in V(T)\) and observe that every in-onion of $x$ and every out-onion of $x$ contains a cycle that crosses one of the cuts induced in $(T,\beta)$ by some edge $e$ of $T$ incident to $x$.
	So this cycle, and therefore also the onion, is hit by \(\gamma(e)\subseteq \theta(x)\).
	
	We finish by providing an upper bound on the width of the decomposition obtained.
	Note that for every edge $e$ of $T$ we have \(\Abs{\gamma(e)} \leqslant d \cdot w\), as it is the union of at most \(w\) edge sets (as \(\Abs{\widehat{\gamma}(e)} \leqslant w\)),	each of size at most \(d\).
	It follows that \(\Abs{\theta(x)} \leqslant 3d \cdot w\) for every node $x$, as the tree \(T=\widehat{T}\) is subcubic.
	Finally, by construction we also have \(\Abs{\beta(x)} \leqslant 1\), providing the desired bound on the width.

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:cycle_hitting}
    Let \(B \in \mathcal{B}\). Suppose \(C\) is a cycle in $D$
    visiting a vertex of \(B\) and of \(V(D) - B\).
    Then \(C\) contains an edge of \(F \cup h(B)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(C\) contains an edge of \(F\) we are immediately done.
    So, assume that \(C\) does not contain any edge of \(F\).
    As \(B\) is the union of a collection of strong components of \(D^\star = (D - F) - Z\),
    and \(C\) visits both a vertex of \(B\) and
    a vertex outside of \(B\), it follows that $C$ must contain a vertex
    of \(Z\).

    Let \(b \in B\) be a vertex visited by \(C\).
    Let \(e\) be an edge in \(C\) that is the last edge before
    \(C\) enters the vertex \(b\) that is an element of \(
	\ifx\relax Z\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\!\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}
                     
	\fi - F\).
    Clearly this edge enters some strong component \(A\) of \(D^\star\),
    and all the edges between $e$ and $b$ along $C$ are contained in \(D^\star\),
    showing that \(b\) is reachable from \(A\) in~$D^\star$.
    This means that the strong component of \(b\) in \(D^\star\)
    is an element of \(\mathcal{R}\). Thus, \(B \neq B_{\mathsf{rest}}\).
    
    Let \(f\) be the first edge of \(C\) occurring
    after \(C\) leaves the vertex \(b\) that is an element of
    \(
	\ifx\relax Z\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{in}_{}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{}\!\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{}\mathchoice{\left( Z \right)}{( Z )}{( Z )}{( Z )}}
                     
	\fi - F\).
    Thus, the strong component of \(b\) in \(D^\star\)
    can reach the edge \(f\) by a path avoiding $F$ or $Z$, and by~\cref{claim:atmost_1_edge}
    it follows that \(B = B_f\), and so \(C\) is hit by \(\set{f} = h(B)\).

head: environment
name: Onion Transport Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
	\[h_k(x)\coloneqq \mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{bip}}(x,
	\ifx\relax k,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( k,2 \right)}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( k,2 \right)}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( k,2 \right)}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( k,2 \right)}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}{( k,2 )}}
                     
	\fi).\]
	We set 
	\begin{align*}
		q_1&\coloneqq h_k(h_k(h_k(h_k(2q))))\\
		q_2&\coloneqq 16\cdot q_1\\
		
	\ifx\relax q,k\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{h}_{\ref{lem:otl}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{h}_{\ref{lem:otl}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( q,k \right)}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{h}_{\ref{lem:otl}}}\mathchoice{\left( q,k \right)}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{h}_{\ref{lem:otl}}}\mathchoice{\left( q,k \right)}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{h}_{\ref{lem:otl}}}\mathchoice{\left( q,k \right)}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}{( q,k )}}
                     
	\fi&\coloneqq q_3\coloneqq h_k(q_2).
	\end{align*}
	Let ${\cal O}=(O_i)_{i\in [q_3]}$ be the family of $q_3$ edge-disjoint onion immersion models with root at $z$ that are assumed to exist. For each $i\in [q_3]$, we let $P^1_i, P^2_i$ be the two trails from $z$ to the tip of $O_i$ within $O_i$, and $P^3_i$ be the trail back from the tip of $O_1$ to $z$ within $O_i$. By shortening the trails if necessary, we may assume that $P^1_i,P^2_i,Q_i$ are paths. For $j\in [2]$, let ${\cal P}^j$ be the set of (pairwise edge-disjoint) trails obtained by taking, for each $i\in [q_3]$, the concatenation of $P^j_i$ and $Q_i$ and removing the last edge. We similarly define families ${\cal Q}^j$ for $j\in [2]$, just from the concatenation of $P^j_i$ and $Q_i$ we remove the first edge instead of the last. Note that each trail from the families ${\cal P}^j,{\cal Q}^j$, $j\in [2]$, visits every vertex at most twice. Moreover, the trails in ${\cal P}^j$ start at $z$ and never visit $z$ again, and the trails in ${\cal Q}^j$ end at $z$ and never visit $z$ before.
	
	Since $z,z'\in Z$ and $Z$ is $q_3$-flow-connected, we may find a family ${\cal K}$ of $q_3$ edge-disjoint paths from $z$ to $z'$ and a family ${\cal L}$ of $q_3$ edge-disjoint paths from $z'$ to $z$. By applying \cref{thm:BipRamsey} (in the bipartite intersection graph of $\cal K$ and $\cal L$) and \cref{lem:onion_harvesting} to ${\cal K}$ and ${\cal L}$, we may assume that all the paths in ${\cal K}\cup {\cal L}$ are pairwise edge-disjoint, at the cost of reducing the sizes of these families to $|{\cal K}|=|{\cal L}|=q_2$. (The other conclusion of the Bipartite Ramsey Theorem (\cref{thm:BipRamsey}) yields, through \cref{lem:onion_harvesting}, an immersion model of an onion-star of order $k$, which is a contradiction.) 
	
	Next, by losing at most half of the paths of ${\cal K}$ and at most half of the onions in ${\cal O}$, we may assume that the edges that the paths of ${\cal K}$ use to leave $z$ are all different from the edges that the paths of ${\cal P}^1$ use to leave $z$. By applying this argument also for the pairs of families $({\cal K},{\cal P}^2)$, $({\cal L},{\cal Q}^1)$, and $({\cal L},{\cal Q}^2)$, we may assume that no path of ${\cal K}$ leaves $z$ using the same edge as a path from ${\cal P}^1\cup {\cal P}^2$, and no path of ${\cal L}$ enters $z$ using the same edge as a path from ${\cal Q}^1\cup {\cal Q}^2$. This is at the cost of restricting ${\cal K}$ and ${\cal L}$ to size at least $q_2/16=q_1$, and ${\cal O}$ to size at least $q_3/16\geqslant q_1$. 
	
	Now, we may apply \cref{thm:BipRamsey} (in the intersection graph) and \cref{lem:onion_harvesting} to the families ${\cal K}$ and ${\cal Q}^1$ in order to assume that the paths in ${\cal K}\cup {\cal Q}^1$ are pairwise edge-disjoint. This is at a cost of losing the inverse of $h$ in the cardinalities of ${\cal K}$ and ${\cal O}$. By performing the same for pairs of families $({\cal K},{\cal Q}^2)$, $({\cal L},{\cal P}^1)$, and $({\cal L},{\cal P}^2)$, we draw the same conclusion about those pairs. This costs restricting ${\cal K}$, ${\cal L}$, and ${\cal O}$ to subfamilies of size $2q$ each.
	
	Now, the paths of ${\cal K}$ and of ${\cal L}$ are all pairwise edge-disjoint, and also edge-disjoint from the onion immersion models in ${\cal O}$. Since $|{\cal K}|=|{\cal L}|=|{\cal O}|=2q$, one can easily match the paths of ${\cal K}$ and ${\cal L}$ with the onions of ${\cal O}$ in order to construct an immersion model of an out-onion-star of order $q$ rooted at $z'$.

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:PH}
	Having a packing of \(S\)-\(T\)-out-tripods of order \(k\cdot z^3\) in \(
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		\mathcal{M}_d
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathcal{M}_d\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi\) yields a packing of \(Z\)-out-tripods of order \(k\) such that they all share the same two sources and the same sink.
	The same holds for in-tripods.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the statement for out-tripods, the arguments for in-tripods are symmetric.
	In fact, this is obtained by a rather simple pigeon-hole-argument.
	
	Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be the packing of \(S\)-\(T\)-out-tripods of order \(k\cdot z^3\).
                                                                                                            
	Each of these sources and the sink of \(P\) correspond to a vertex in \(Z\), by construction of \(
	\ifx\relax D\relax
		\mathcal{M}_d
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathcal{M}_d\!\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}{\mathcal{M}_d\mathchoice{\left( D \right)}{( D )}{( D )}{( D )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	So we consider the projection \(P_Z\) of \(P\) into \(D\), replacing the edges in \(P\cap 
	\ifx\relax S\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{out}_{D'}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{D'}\!\mathchoice{\left( S \right)}{( S )}{( S )}{( S )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( S \right)}{( S )}{( S )}{( S )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( S \right)}{( S )}{( S )}{( S )}}{\partial^\mathsf{out}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( S \right)}{( S )}{( S )}{( S )}}
                     
	\fi\) by out-edges from \(Z\) in \(D\) and the edge in \(P\cap 
	\ifx\relax T\relax
		\partial^\mathsf{in}_{D'}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{D'}\!\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}{\partial^\mathsf{in}_{D'}\mathchoice{\left( T \right)}{( T )}{( T )}{( T )}}
                     
	\fi\) by the corresponding in-edge into \(Z\) in \(D\).
	Note that \(P_Z\) is a \(Z\)-tripod and let \(\mathcal{P}_Z = \Set{P_Z\mid P\in \mathcal{P}}\) be the packing of \(Z\)-onions obtained.
	
	To simplify the argument assume that the \(Z\)-onions have a \emph{first} and a \emph{second} source, that is, making them distinguishable in an arbitrary way.
	
	As there is only \(z\) vertices in \(Z\), there is a vertex \(z_1 \in Z\) such that \(k\cdot z^2\) members \(\mathcal{P}_1\) of \(\mathcal{P}_Z\) have \(z_1\) as their first sources.
	Similarly, there is a vertex \(z_2 \in Z\) such that \(k\cdot z\) members \(\mathcal{P}_2\) of \(\mathcal{P}_1\) have \(z_2\) as their second source.
	
	Finally, there is a vertex \(z_3 \in Z\) such that \(k\) members \(\mathcal{P}_3\) of \(\mathcal{P}_2\) have \(z_3\) as their sink.
	
	Thus, the claim holds.

label: claim:uncross
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:uncross}
  There exists a function \(h : \mathds{N} \rightarrow \mathds{N}\) such that the following holds.

  Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be a set of edge-disjoint \(Z\)-out-tripods in \(D\),
  all of which have
  the same vertex \(z \in Z\) as sink, and let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a set of pairwise
  edge-disjoint trails in \(D\), all starting at \(z\).

  Then, for any positive integer \(n\), if
  \(\size*{\mathcal{T}} \geqslant h(n)\),
  and \(\size*{\mathcal{P}} \geqslant h(n)\),
  then either
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \(D\) contains an immersion of an onion star of order \(2k^2\), or
    \item there exists a subsets \(\mathcal{T}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{P}' \subseteq \mathcal{P}\),
      each of size \(n\),
      such that each tripod in \(\mathcal{T}'\) is edge-disjoint
      from every trail in \(\mathcal{P}'\).
  \end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set 
  \begin{equation*}
    h(n) = \mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{bip}}(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi, \mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{bip}}(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi, n)).
  \end{equation*}
  Construct two sets of trails \(\mathcal{Q}_1 = \set{Q^1_T : T \in \mathcal{T}}, \mathcal{Q}_2 = \set{Q^2_T : T \in \mathcal{T}}\) indexed by \(\mathcal{T}\)
  as follows:
  for each \(Z\)-out-tripod \(T \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{out}}\) with the centre \(c \in V(D) - Z\),
  let \(L_1\) be the \(z_1\)-\(c\) path contained in \(T\) where \(z_1 \in Z\) is one
  of the sources of~\(T\),
  let \(L_2\) be the \(z_2\)-\(c\) path contained in \(T\)
  where \(z_2\) is the second source of~\(T\),
  and let \(R\) be the \(c\)-\(z_3\) trail contained in \(T\);
  add \(Q^1_T\) defined as the concatenation of \(L_1\) and \(R\) to~\(\mathcal{Q}_1\),
  and~\(Q^2_T\) the concatenation of \(L_2\) and~\(R\) to~\(\mathcal{Q}_2\).
  Thus, each of \(\set{\mathcal{Q}_1, \mathcal{Q}_2}\) is a set of pairwise edge-disjoint
  trails in \(D\) all terminating at \(z\).

  Build an auxiliary bipartite graph on \(\mathcal{T} \cup \mathcal{P}\) as follows:
  \(T \in \mathcal{T}\) and \(P \in \mathcal{P}\) are adjacent if and only if~\(Q^1_T\) and~\(P\) share an edge.
  By~\cref{thm:BipRamsey}, either there is a complete bipartite
  subgraph of size at least \(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi\)
  or an anti-complete bipartite subgraph of size at least \(\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{bip}}(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi, n)\).

  Assume we are in the former case.
  Thus, we have a subset \(\mathcal{T}_c \subseteq \mathcal{T}\),
  and \(\mathcal{P}_c \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) such that for each \(T \in \mathcal{T}_c\) and \(P \in \mathcal{P}_c\),
  the trails~\(Q^1_T\) and~\(P\) share an edge, and each is of size \(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi\).
  This is exactly the setup of~\cref{lem:onion_harvesting},
  and in this case we conclude that \(D\) contains an onion star immersion
  of order~\(2k^2\).

  In the latter case, we have \(\mathcal{T}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{T}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) such that for each \(T \in \mathcal{T}_0\) and \(P \in \mathcal{P}_0\),
  the trails~\(Q^1_T\) and~\(P\) are edge-disjoint,
  and each is of size \(\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{bip}}(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi, n)\).
  Now, build another auxiliary bipartite graph on~\(\mathcal{T}_0 \cup \mathcal{P}_0\),
  but now instead focus on \(Q_2\):
  \(T \in \mathcal{T}_0\) and \(P \in \mathcal{P}_0\) are adjacent if and only if
  \(Q^2_T\) and \(P\) share an edge.

  By~\cref{thm:BipRamsey}, either there is a complete bipartite
  subgraph of size at least \(
	\ifx\relax 2k^2,2\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{lem:onion_harvesting}}}\mathchoice{\left( 2k^2,2 \right)}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}{( 2k^2,2 )}}
                     
	\fi\)
  or a anti-complete bipartite subgraph of size at least \(n\).

  The former case unfolds exactly as in the previous
  step, with~\cref{lem:onion_harvesting} yielding a
  onion star immersion of order \(2k^2\).
  In the latter case, we obtain the desired subsets,
  as each tripod \(T\) is edge-covered by the two paths \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\).

body_md:
Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be the two \(u\)-\(v\)-trails and \(P_3\) be the \(v\)-\(u\)-trail of a minimal \((F,(X,Y))\)-quasi-onion with root \(u \in X\) and tip \(v \in Y\).
	Note that the minimality asserts that $P_1,P_2$ and $P_3$ are paths. Also, note that since $P_1,P_2,P_3$ constitute a \((F,(X,Y))\)-quasi-onion, every edge shared by two of those trails must have both endpoints in $X$ (\emph{lie} in $X$) or both endpoints in $Y$ (\emph{lie} in $Y$).
	
	First we show that \(P_1\) is disjoint from \(P_2\).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                 
                                                           
	Assume otherwise and consider the first edge \(f \in F\) along \(P_1\) that it shares with \(P_2\).
	If \(f\) lies in \(Y\), then we define \(v' \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax f\relax
		\mathsf{tail}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{tail}\!\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}
                     
	\fi\) as the new tip and \(P'_1 \coloneqq P_1v'\), \(P'_2 \coloneqq P_2v'\) and \(P'_3 \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax v'P_2 \cdot P_3\relax
		\mathsf{red}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{red}\!\mathchoice{\left( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 \right)}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 \right)}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 \right)}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 \right)}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}{( v'P_2 \cdot P_3 )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	This way the overall number of edges drops by the number of edges in \(v'P_1\) which is at least 1, as it contains \(f\).                                            
	The paths \(P'_1,P'_2\) and \(P'_3\) therefore yield a smaller $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion with root \(u\) and tip \(v'\), a contradiction.
	
	If \(f\) lies in \(X\), then we define \(u' \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax f\relax
		\mathsf{head}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{head}\!\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}
                     
	\fi\) as the new root.
	Then, we define \(P'_1 \coloneqq u'P_1\), \(P'_2 \coloneqq u'P_2\) and \(P'_3 \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax P_3 \cdot P_1u\relax
		\mathsf{red}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{red}\!\mathchoice{\left( P_3 \cdot P_1u \right)}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_3 \cdot P_1u \right)}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_3 \cdot P_1u \right)}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_3 \cdot P_1u \right)}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}{( P_3 \cdot P_1u )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	Again, we obtain a smaller $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion (by the number of edges in \(P_2u'\), in particular $f$) with root \(u'\) and tip \(v\), a contradiction.
	
	So, we may assume that the paths \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are indeed edge-disjoint.
	We continue to consider the possibility of \(P_i\) intersecting \(P_3\) for \(i \in [2]\).
	Let \(j \coloneqq 3-i\).

	Consider the first intersection edge \(f \in F\) along \(P_i\) with \(P_3\).
	If \(f\) lies in \(Y\), then we define \(v' \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax f\relax
		\mathsf{tail}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{tail}\!\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}
                     
	\fi\) as the new tip.
	Then, we choose \(P'_i \coloneqq P_iv'\), \(P'_j \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax P_j \cdot P_3v'\relax
		\mathsf{red}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{red}\!\mathchoice{\left( P_j \cdot P_3v' \right)}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_j \cdot P_3v' \right)}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_j \cdot P_3v' \right)}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( P_j \cdot P_3v' \right)}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}{( P_j \cdot P_3v' )}}
                     
	\fi\) and \(P'_3 \coloneqq v'P_3\).
	This yields a smaller $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion, a contradiction.
	
	If \(f\) lies in \(X\), then we define \(u' \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax f\relax
		\mathsf{head}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{head}\!\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}{\mathsf{head}\mathchoice{\left( f \right)}{( f )}{( f )}{( f )}}
                     
	\fi\) and \(P'_i \coloneqq u'P_i\), \(P'_j \coloneqq 
	\ifx\relax u'P_3\cdot P_j\relax
		\mathsf{red}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{red}\!\mathchoice{\left( u'P_3\cdot P_j \right)}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( u'P_3\cdot P_j \right)}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( u'P_3\cdot P_j \right)}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}}{\mathsf{red}\mathchoice{\left( u'P_3\cdot P_j \right)}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}{( u'P_3\cdot P_j )}}
                     
	\fi\) and \(P'_3 \coloneqq P_3u'\).
	This again would yield a smaller $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion, a contradiction.
	
	So, indeed, the three paths \(P_1,P_2\) and \(P_3\) are all edge-disjoint and thus form an actual immersion model of an onion.

If $x$ is a leaf of $\widehat{T}$, there is nothing to prove, so assume that $y_1,\ldots, y_\ell$ are the children of $x$ in $\widehat{T}$. 
		For every $i \in [\ell]$, let \(t_i \in 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) be such that \(a_i \in \beta^0_x(t_i)\) and let \(t'_i \in 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) be such that \(b_i \in \beta^0_x(t'_i)\).
		Let \(P_i\) be the unique \(t_i\)-\(t'_i\)-path in \(T^0_x\).
		
		Recall that we denote by $O_i$ the onion consisting of the three edges between $a_i$ and $b_i$.

	\begin{claim}
		\label{claim:edge_guards_splitting_contain_aux_edge}
		If \(e \in 
	\ifx\relax P_i\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}
                     
	\fi\), then \(\gamma^0_x(e)\) contains at least one of the auxiliary edges \(
	\ifx\relax O_i\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	\end{claim}
	\begin{claimproof}
		This follows from \(O_i\) containing a cycle that visits \(a_i\) and \(b_i\), which  crosses \(e\) and thus has to be hit by the edge-guard \(\gamma^0_x(e)\).
	\end{claimproof}
	
	\begin{claim}
		\label{claim:onion_guards_splitting_contain_aux_edge}
		If \(t \in 
	\ifx\relax P_i\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}
                     
	\fi-\Set{t_i,t'_i}\), then \(\theta^0_x(t)\) contains at least one of the auxiliary edges \(
	\ifx\relax O_i\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( O_i \right)}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}{( O_i )}}
                     
	\fi\).
	\end{claim}
	\begin{claimproof}
		This follows from \(O_i\) containing an onion with tip \(a_i\) and root \(b_i\), which crosses \(t\) and thus has to be hit by the onion-guard \(\theta^0_x(t)\).
	\end{claimproof}
		
		We define \(T_x \coloneqq T^0_x\).
		Then, for every \(t \in 
	\ifx\relax T_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}
                     
	\fi = 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) we define 
		\begin{equation*}
			\beta_x(t) \coloneqq \beta^0_x(t)-\Set{b_i\mid a_i \not\in \beta^0_x(t)} \cup \Set{b_i\mid a_i \in \beta^0_x(t).}
		\end{equation*}
		That is, we move each auxiliary vertex \(b_i\) to the bag containing \(a_i\).
		This increases the size of the bags at most by a factor of two.
		
		
		For every \(e \in 
	\ifx\relax T_x\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}
                     
	\fi = 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) we define
		\begin{equation*}
			\gamma_x(e) \coloneqq \gamma^0_x(e) \cup \Set{\mathchoice{\left( a_i,b_i \right)}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}\mid e\in
	\ifx\relax P_i\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}
                     
	\fi}.
		\end{equation*}
		The size of the edge-guard of $e$ grows by the number of paths \(P_i\) the edge $e$ lies on.
	By~\cref{claim:edge_guards_splitting_contain_aux_edge}, these are at most as many as the original edge-guard size.
	So, the edge-guards grow by at most a factor two.
		
		Similarly, for every \(t \in 
	\ifx\relax T_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}
                     
	\fi = 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T^0_x \right)}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}{( T^0_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) we define
		\begin{equation*}
			\theta_x(t) \coloneqq \theta^0_x(t) \cup \Set{\mathchoice{\left( a_i,b_i \right)}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}\mid t \in 
	\ifx\relax P_i\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}
                     
	\fi}.
	\end{equation*}
	Each onion-guard grows by one edge for every \(P_i\) its corresponding node $t$ in $T_x=T_x^0$ lies on.
	Thus, if we denote by $n_i$ and $n_e$, respectively, the number of paths $P_i$ that contain $t$ as an internal vertex, and as an endpoint, we have $|\theta_x(t)| \leqslant |\theta^0_x(t)| + n_i + n_e$. 
	If $t$ is an internal node of \(P_i\), by~\cref{claim:onion_guards_splitting_contain_aux_edge}, $\theta_x^0(t)$ already contains an edge from \(O_i\), thus $n_i \leqslant |\theta^0_x(t)|$.
	Note that $t$ can be only an endpoint of \(P_i\) if $\beta^0_x(t)$ contains \(a_i\) or \(b_i\). Therefore, $n_e \leqslant |\beta^0_x(t)|$.
	Thus, the new onion-guards are at most twice their original size plus the maximum bag-size, i.e.~three times the width of $\mathcal{T}^0_x$.
	
	It remains to show that both the new edge-guards and the new onion-guards are doing their job in hitting all crossing cycles or onions.
	Let \(e\in 
	\ifx\relax T_x\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}
                     
	\fi\) be an edge in the decomposition and \(C\) be a cycle of \(\mathsf{tor}(D,x)\) crossing \(e\).
	If \(C\) is a cycle crossing \(e\) in \(\mathcal{T}^0_x\) as well, then it is hit by \(\gamma^0_x(e) \subseteq \gamma_x(e)\).
	If \(C\) does not cross \(e\) in \(\mathcal{T}^0_x\), then there is \(i \in [\ell]\) such that \(e \in 
	\ifx\relax P_i\relax
		E
	\else
		\mathchoice{E\!\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}{E\mathchoice{\left( P_i \right)}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}{( P_i )}}
                     
	\fi\) and \(C\) visits \(b_i\). Thus, $C$ contains the edge \(\mathchoice{\left( a_i,b_i \right)}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}{( a_i,b_i )}\), which ensures that $C$ is hit by \(\gamma_x(e)\).
	
	For the onion-guards, let \(t \in 
	\ifx\relax T^0_x\relax

If $e$ is an outer edge, for some $(x, x') \in E(\widehat{T})$ such that $t \in V(T_x)$, and $t' \in V(T_{x'})$, we have \(\beta({T}^{t}_{e}) = \widehat{\beta}({{\widehat{T}}}^{x}_{e})\) and \(\beta({T}^{t'}_{e}) = \widehat{\beta}({{\widehat{T}}}^{x'}_{e})\), so the statement follows because $\gamma(e)=\widehat\gamma(x,x')$.
	
	Suppose now $e$ is an inner edge. Let $x$ be such that $t,t' \in V(T_x)$, and \(C\) be a cycle visiting vertices from the bags of both \({T}^{t}_{e}\) and of \({T}^{t'}_{e}\).
	
	If \(C\) visits a vertex that lies in \(\widehat{\beta}({T}^{\uparrow}_{x})\), then it has to contain an edge from \(\widehat{\gamma}\mathchoice{\left( x',x \right)}{( x',x )}{( x',x )}{( x',x )}\), where \(x'\) is the parent of \(x\), by~\cref{item:tp:edgeguards}, so it is hit by \(\widehat{\gamma}\mathchoice{\left( x',x \right)}{( x',x )}{( x',x )}{( x',x )} \subseteq \gamma(e)\).
	
	                                                                                              
	
	So we can assume that $C$ does not visit vertices from \(\widehat{\beta}({T}^{\uparrow}_{x})\).
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
	We consider a subgraph of $\mathsf{tor}(D,x)$ induced by all edges of the form $\mathsf{origin}^{-1}_x(e)$, for every edge $e \in E(C)$ for which $\mathsf{origin}^{-1}_x(e)$ exists, and edges $(a_i,b_i)$ for every child $y_i$ of $x$ in $\widehat{T}$ such that $C$ intersects $\beta({T}^{\downarrow}_{y_i})$.
	This subgraph includes a cycle $C'$ that, if there exists $y_i$ such that $C$ intersects $\beta({T}^{\downarrow}_{y_i})$, contains the auxiliary edge $(a_i,b_i)$. If there is no such $y_i$, consider $C'=C$, as $C$ is a cycle in $D[\widehat\beta(x)]\subseteq \mathsf{tor}(D,x)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(x \in V(\widehat{T})\) be such that \(t \in 
	\ifx\relax T_x\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( T_x \right)}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}{( T_x )}}
                     
	\fi\).
		Note that each onion immersion model for which either root or tip is outside of the bags of the subtree of $\widehat{T}$ rooted at \(x\), and the other one is inside, is hit by \(\widehat{\gamma}(x',x)\), where $x'$ is the parent of $x$ in $\widehat{T}$.
		So we only need to consider those onions that completely live in the subtree of $\widehat{T}$ rooted at \(x\).
		For these we make use of the Quasi-onion Lemma~(\cref{lem:quasi_onions}).
		
		Assume in the decomposition $\mathcal{T}_x$ of $\mathsf{tor}(D,x)$, the onion-guard \(\theta_x(t)\) hits all out-onions of \(t\).
		We aim to show that then \(\theta(t)\) also hits all out-onions of \(t\) in $\mathcal{T}$.
		Let \(O\) be an out-onion of $t$ in $\mathcal{T}$ (so $O$ is an onion immersion model in $D$) and let \(P_1,P_2,P_3\) be the three trails forming it.
		Let \(F \coloneqq \Set{(a_i,b_i) \mid y_i \text{ is a child of } x}\).
		As the mapping $\mathsf{origin}_{x}$ is a bijection, passing $P_1,P_2,P_3$ through $\mathsf{origin}_{x}$ and augmenting them with the edges of $F$, if necessary, naturally yields an \((F,(X,Y))\)-quasi-onion \(O'\) in \(\mathsf{tor}(D,x)\), for any cut $(X,Y)$ such that the root is in $X$ and the tip is in $Y$.
		
		If the root of \(O\) lies within \(\beta(t)\), then consider the bipartition \((X,Y) \coloneqq (\beta(t), 
	\ifx\relax \mathsf{tor}(D,x)\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}
                     
	\fi-\beta(t))\).
		Otherwise, let \(t'\) be the neighbour of \(t\) such that the bags of the subtree \((T_x)^{tt'}_{t'}\) contain the root of \(O\), then consider the bipartition \((X,Y) \coloneqq (\beta_x((T_x)^{tt'}_{t'}),
	\ifx\relax \mathsf{tor}(D,x)\relax
		V
	\else
		\mathchoice{V\!\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}{V\mathchoice{\left( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) \right)}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}{( \mathsf{tor}(D,x) )}}
                     
	\fi-\beta_x((T_x)^{tt'}_{t'}))\). Note that no edge of $F$ crosses the cut $(X,Y)$, and hence $O'$ is an $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion.
		
		Now let \(O''\) be the minimal $(F,(X,Y))$-quasi-onion contained in the union of the paths of \(O'\) that has its root in $X$ and tip in $Y$.
		By~\cref{lem:quasi_onions}, \(O''\) is an onion and in particular, by our choice of \((X,Y)\), an out-onion of \(t\) in $\mathcal{T}_x$. Therefore, $O''$ is hit by \(\theta_x(t)\).
		
		If the intersection of \(O''\) and \(\theta_x(t)\) contains an edge $e$ that is not an auxiliary edge in $\mathsf{tor}(D,x)$, then $\mathsf{origin}_{x}(e)$ also lies in \(\theta(t)\) and hits \(O\).
		Otherwise, \(O\) is hit by the set \(\bigcup\Set{\widehat{\gamma}(x,c_i) \mid i\in [\ell] \text{ and }\theta_x(t)\cap E(O_i)\neq \emptyset}\), which was included in $\theta(t)$.

Define functions $g_c$ and $f_c$ by:

	\fi\right)^{ck+k}\right\rceil\right\}, \\ f_c(k)&=\max\left\{3k(c+1),3\cdot\left\lceil\frac14(36 \cdot 
	\ifx\relax g_c(k)\relax
		\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{thm:kst}}}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{thm:kst}}}\!\mathchoice{\left( g_c(k) \right)}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{thm:kst}}}\mathchoice{\left( g_c(k) \right)}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{thm:kst}}}\mathchoice{\left( g_c(k) \right)}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}}{\textcolor{green!50!black}{\mathsf{g}_{\ref{thm:kst}}}\mathchoice{\left( g_c(k) \right)}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}{( g_c(k) )}}
                     
	\fi)^{g_c(k)}\right\rceil\right\}.
\end{align*}
Fix $Q \in \mathcal{Q}$, and let $e$ be the $<_Q$-smallest arc of $Q$ such that the number of paths in $\mathcal{P}$ that have a common arc with the suffix of $Q$ that starts in $\mathsf{next}_Q(e)$ equals $|\mathcal{P}|/3$. 
                                                                             
Let $\bar{Q}$ be the suffix of $Q$ that starts in $e$.

\textbf{Case 1.} Suppose that $\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})=\{P \in \mathcal{P} \mid A(P) \cap A(\bar{Q})\}$ contains at least two $\bar{Q}$-dangerous paths. 
Let $d$ be the $<_Q$-greatest dangerous crossing in $Q$ and let $P_2$ be the path such that $d$ is a $(P_2,Q)$-crossing. 
Then $d$ belongs to $\bar{Q}$.
Let $e'$ be the $<_Q$-greatest dangerous crossing in $A(Q)- A(P_2)$ and let $P_1\in\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})-\{P_2\}$ be the path such that $e'$ is a $(P_1,Q)$-crossing (with possibly $e=e'$).
Let $d'$ be the $<_{P_2}$-smallest $(P_2,Q)$-crossing belonging to the suffix of $Q$ that starts with $\mathsf{next}_Q(e')$.
Clearly since $d$ is dangerous and belongs to $\bar{Q}$, $d'$ must be dangerous (with possibly $d=d'$). 

Let $y=
	\ifx\relax d'\relax
		\mathsf{tail}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{tail}\!\mathchoice{\left( d' \right)}{( d' )}{( d' )}{( d' )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( d' \right)}{( d' )}{( d' )}{( d' )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( d' \right)}{( d' )}{( d' )}{( d' )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( d' \right)}{( d' )}{( d' )}{( d' )}}
                     
	\fi$.
We consider the $(x,y)$-trails: one that goes along $P_1$ to $e'$ and then continues along $Q$ to $y$, and the other that goes along $P_2$, and the $(y,x)$-trail that goes along $Q$.
All of these are arc-disjoint.
Now the minimal $(x,y)$-trails/$(y,x)$-trail contained in the above (as $y$ may occur more than one on each of them) form an onion immersion model with root $x$ and tip $y$.

Let $\mathcal{Q}^\circ \subseteq \mathcal{Q}$ be the set of trails which are arc-disjoint both with the prefix of $P_1$ that ends with $e'$ and the prefix of $P_2$ that ends with $d'$ (so in particular $Q\notin \mathcal{Q}^\circ$).
Since $e'$ and $d'$ are both dangerous, $|\mathcal{Q}^\circ|> |\mathcal{Q}|-|\mathcal{Q}|/3-|\mathcal{Q}|/3=|\mathcal{Q}|/3\geqslant (c+1)k$.
Let us pick an arbitrary collection $\mathcal{P}^*\subseteq\mathcal{P}- \{P_1,P_2\}$ of $k$ trails that are arc-disjoint with the suffix of $Q$ that starts with $e'$.
Such a collection exists, as the number of trails in $\mathcal{P}$ that intersect the suffix of $Q$ that starts with $\mathsf{next}_Q(e)$ equals $|\mathcal{P}|/3$, yielding $\smash{\frac23}|\mathcal{P}|\geqslant 2(c+1)k$ candidate trails for $\mathcal{P}^*$.
Since each trail in such a collection has at most $c$ arcs whose tail is $y$ (as each vertex occurs at most $c$ times on each trail), there are at most $c|\mathcal{P}^*|=ck$ arcs in $A(\mathcal{Q}^\circ)\cap A(\mathcal{P}^*)$ whose tail is $y$. Let $\mathcal{Q}^*\subseteq \mathcal{Q}^\circ$ comprise any $n$ trails disjoint with these arcs.
Clearly, since $\mathcal{P}^* \subseteq \mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^* \subseteq \mathcal{Q}$, $(\mathcal{P}^*,\mathcal{Q}^*)$ is a well-crossing pair. Hence $\pi$, $\mathcal{P}^*$ and $\mathcal{Q}^*$ satisfy all the desired properties.

\textbf{Case 2.} Suppose that there is at most one $\bar{Q}$-dangerous path in $\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})$. 
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of those trails in $\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})$ whose all crossings with $\bar{Q}$ are safe, and let $\bar{\mathcal{S}}$ be the set of trails from $\mathcal{S}$ trimmed so that they start at $x$, have no arcs in common with $\bar{Q}$ and are maximally long.
Since $|\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})| = |\mathcal{P}|/3+1$ and there is at most one dangerous trail in $\mathcal{P}(\bar{Q})$, we derive $|\bar{\mathcal{S}}|\geqslant|\mathcal{P}|/3$. 

\begin{claim}[\cite{bozyk2022digraphs}]\label{cla:same-paths}
There exist subfamilies $\bar{\mathcal{S}}'\subseteq \bar{\mathcal{S}}$, $\mathcal{Q}'\subseteq \mathcal{Q}- \{Q\}$ such that $|\bar{\mathcal{S}}'|=g_c(k)$, $|\mathcal{Q}'|=g_c(k)$ and $(\bar{\mathcal{S}}',\mathcal{Q}')$ is well-crossing with congestion $c$ rooted at $x$.
\end{claim}

Consider the pair $(\bar{\mathcal{S}}',\mathcal{Q}')$ given by \cref{cla:same-paths} and
let $\mathcal{S}'$ be the set of paths in $\mathcal{S}$ from which $\bar{\mathcal{S}}'$ originates (i.e., the paths from $\bar{\mathcal{S}}'$ before trimming).
              
\begin{claim}[\cite{bozyk2022digraphs}]\label{cla:paths}
There exist 
\begin{itemize}
\item distinct $P_1,P_2 \in \mathcal{S}'$, 
\item a subfamily $\mathcal{P}^\circ$ of $\bar{\mathcal{S}}'$, and 
\item a subfamily $\mathcal{Q}^\circ$ of the set $\bar{\mathcal{Q}}'$ of trails from $\mathcal{Q}'$ trimmed so that they end at $x$, have no arcs in common with $P_1$ or $P_2$ and are longest possible, 
\end{itemize}
such that $|\mathcal{P}^\circ| = |\mathcal{Q}^\circ| = (c+1)k$ and $(\mathcal{P}^\circ,\mathcal{Q}^\circ)$ is well-crossing with congestion $c$ rooted at~$x$.\footnotemark                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                         
\end{claim}
                            
                                           
\footnotetext{The proof of \cref{cla:paths} in \cite{bozyk2022digraphs} uses the definition of $g_c$ for $c=1$, but the correctness of calculations for the more general case is straightforward to verify.}
                       
             

Consider $P_1$, $P_2$ and $(\mathcal{P}^\circ,\mathcal{Q}^\circ)$ as in the claim above and denote
$e_i=\min_{<_{P_i}}\{A(\bar{Q})\cap A(P_i)\}$ for $i=1,2$. 
Assume without loss of generality that $e_1<_Q e_2$, i.e., that the $<_{P_1}$-smallest $(P_1,\bar{Q})$-crossing is further from $x$ on $\bar{Q}$ than the $<_{P_2}$-smallest $(P_2,\bar{Q})$-crossing. Let $y=
	\ifx\relax e_2\relax
		\mathsf{tail}
	\else
		\mathchoice{\mathsf{tail}\!\mathchoice{\left( e_2 \right)}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( e_2 \right)}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( e_2 \right)}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}}{\mathsf{tail}\mathchoice{\left( e_2 \right)}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}{( e_2 )}}
                     
	\fi$.
By the choice of $e_1$ and $e_2$, we have two $(x,y)$-trails: the one that goes along $P_1$ to $e_1$ and then continues along $Q$ to $y$, and the one that is a prefix of $P_2$, and one $(y,x)$-trail that is a suffix of $Q$.
All of these are pairwise arc-disjoint.
Now the minimal $(x,y)$-trails/$(y,x)$-trail contained in the above form an onion-immersion with root $x$ and tip $y$. 

The last step (to ensure that $y$ will not be the tail of a crossing in the found well-crossing pair) is performed similarly as in the first case: we pick an arbitrary collection $\mathcal{P}^\ast$ of exactly $k$ trails among the $(c+1)n$ paths in $\mathcal{P}^\circ$, and select a subfamily $\mathcal{Q}^\ast$ consisting of $k$ trails which do not contain crossings of tail $y$ among the $(c+1)k$ trails in $\mathcal{Q}^\circ$.
